section_summary: This section combines filing and cross-reference sheets, U.S. diplomatic and law-enforcement correspondence, advocacy by the Foreign Policy Association, and extensive official reports on narcotics in Japan and Japanese-controlled territories. The 1937 League of Nations report covers regulation, addiction treatment, cultivation, manufacture, seizures, illicit traffic, and prepared-opium monopolies in Japan, Korea, Taiwan, the Kwantung Leased Territory, the South Sea Islands, Hankow, and Tientsin. The section closes with the Japan Proper portion of the Japanese Government’s corresponding report for 1938.

subfiles.title: File jacket: Traffic in Narcotics—Japan, Jacket No. 7
subfiles.about: The jacket cover identifies the case as concerning traffic in narcotics in Japan.
subfiles.summary: This is the administrative cover for Jacket No. 7 of the narcotics case. It bears the subject, date, case markings, and instructions not to remove or disarrange the papers.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to report on the Tsinan narcotics situation
subfiles.about: The sheet cross-references a report that a Japanese official urged an American automobile-company manager to enter the more profitable opium trade.
subfiles.summary: This filing note points to a document concerning narcotics conditions in Tsinan. Its précis states that a Japanese official advised the American manager of a local branch of an American company to abandon automobiles for the lucrative opium trade.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 3796: Army Participation in Drug Traffic
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: The Embassy answers an inquiry concerning allegations that Japanese army officers had published material acknowledging Japanese involvement in narcotics traffic in China.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports that the allegation probably derived from General Tada’s suppressed 1935 statement criticizing Japanese misconduct in China, including narcotics manufacture, secret sales, and smuggling. He quotes related passages transmitted in earlier Peiping and Tokyo despatches. The Embassy found no additional army pamphlets of the kind described in the New York Herald Tribune editorial.

subfiles.title: Confidential transmittal of Despatch No. 3796 to the Treasury Department
subfiles.about: The State Department confidentially forwards the Tokyo despatch and newspaper editorial concerning alleged Japanese Army participation in narcotics trafficking.
subfiles.summary: The note encloses duplicate copies of Embassy Despatch No. 3796 and the November 29, 1938 New York Herald Tribune editorial. The material is supplied for the confidential information of the Treasury Department and its Customs Agency Service.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference concerning a narcotics exhibit at the San Francisco World’s Fair
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to Japanese consular objections to an exhibit depicting Japan as a principal source of narcotics.
subfiles.summary: This filing note directs the reader to another file concerning a narcotics exhibit at the San Francisco World’s Fair. It records the Japanese consul’s objection to a display indicating that Japan was one of the principal sources of supply.

subfiles.title: Letter transmitting a memorandum translated from El Siglo de Torreón
subfiles.from: J. Edgar Hoover, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.about: Hoover forwards a confidential source’s memorandum translating a Mexican newspaper article about narcotics trafficking.
subfiles.summary: Hoover sends a copy of a memorandum headed as a translation from the April 8 issue of El Siglo de Torreón. He notes that the same information was supplied to Narcotics Commissioner H. J. Anslinger.

subfiles.title: Translation from El Siglo de Torreón, issue of April 8
subfiles.about: The garbled translated article alleges cross-border opium trafficking from Mexico into the United States and suggests German and Japanese involvement.
subfiles.summary: The surviving OCR describes seizures of three-kilogram opium shipments and the arrest of Gustavo Escamilla at Douglas. It claims that opium was coming directly from Mexico for carriage to the United States and advances an allegation of German-Japanese activity connected with narcotics production or trafficking in Mexico. Much of the page is badly corrupted, so its finer details remain uncertain.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Hoover’s May 9 letter
subfiles.about: The State Department acknowledges the FBI material about illicit narcotics traffic from Mexico to the United States.
subfiles.summary: The note thanks the Attorney General for Hoover’s letter and the accompanying translation from El Siglo de Torreón. It identifies the subject as illicit narcotics trafficking from Mexico into the United States.

subfiles.title: List of League of Nations documents forwarded from Geneva
subfiles.about: The Consulate lists copies of Japan’s 1937 annual opium report sent to Washington and Bern.
subfiles.summary: The sheet identifies League of Nations document C.130.M.82.1939.XI, Japan’s annual report for 1937. Four copies were sent to the Department of State, with additional copies distributed to the American Legation at Bern and the communications and records division.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Japan’s 1937 narcotics report to the Treasury Department
subfiles.about: The State Department forwards Japan’s official 1937 report on opium and dangerous drugs to Treasury agencies.
subfiles.summary: The note encloses Japan’s annual report submitted under the 1931 Narcotics Limitation Convention and transmitted by the League of Nations Secretary-General. Additional copies are provided for the Bureau of Narcotics, Public Health Service, and Customs Agency Service.

subfiles.title: League of Nations Annual Reports by Governments for 1937—Japan
subfiles.from: Government of Japan, communicated by the Secretary-General of the League of Nations
subfiles.to: Parties to the 1931 Convention and the Advisory Committee on Traffic in Opium and Other Dangerous Drugs
subfiles.about: The report presents official Japanese statistics and policies on opium and narcotics in Japan and its colonies, mandates, leased territory, and concessions.
subfiles.summary: The report covers laws, administrative controls, addiction treatment, cultivation, manufacture, international trade, prosecutions, confiscations, and illicit traffic during 1937 in Japan Proper, Korea, Taiwan, the Kwantung Leased Territory, and the South Sea Islands. Special sections describe prepared-opium systems in Taiwan and Kwantung, including licensed smokers, government monopolies, revenues, treatment, and seizures. Reports from the Japanese concessions at Hankow and Tientsin record arrests, confiscated drugs, illicit prices, and authorized medical users. It also describes the Heian Maru smuggling case and Japanese-American cooperation surrounding it.

subfiles.title: Letter introducing Mrs. Howell Moorhead
subfiles.from: Frank R. McCoy, Foreign Policy Association
subfiles.about: McCoy asks Secretary Hull to receive Mrs. Howell Moorhead so she can present the Opium Research Committee’s views.
subfiles.summary: McCoy identifies Moorhead as director of the Foreign Policy Association’s opium work. He notes that the committee had worked since 1922 with the Geneva opium bodies and had published pamphlets useful to the State Department.

subfiles.title: Foreign Policy Association memorandum on narcotics in Japanese-controlled China
subfiles.from: Mrs. Howell Moorhead and the Opium Research Committee, Foreign Policy Association
subfiles.about: The committee urges the United States to raise Japan’s treaty obligations concerning opium and dangerous drugs in any bilateral discussions.
subfiles.summary: The committee argues that evidence presented at Geneva showed worsening narcotics conditions in Japanese-controlled areas of China. Although smuggling to the United States from Japanese ships had declined, it says clandestine manufacture and illicit distribution remained widespread in occupied China. It recommends asking Japan to fulfill its narcotics-treaty obligations and predicts favorable American public support for such action.

subfiles.title: Counselor’s memorandum on Mrs. Moorhead’s visit
subfiles.about: Moore records Moorhead’s proposal that narcotics be included in negotiations with Japan or addressed independently.
subfiles.summary: Moore recounts a conversation in which Moorhead urged that the narcotics issue be included in any negotiations over American-Japanese problems. She also believed Japan might consider narcotics separately and stressed preventing existing control measures from becoming ineffective. Moore expected Fuller to consider the matter and communicate with her.

subfiles.title: Reply to General McCoy concerning the Foreign Policy Association proposal
subfiles.from: R. Walton Moore, Counselor of the Department of State
subfiles.about: Moore acknowledges the Association’s letters and assures McCoy that the Department carefully considers its narcotics-control proposals.
subfiles.summary: Moore explains that Mrs. Moorhead delivered McCoy’s November 17 letter and the committee’s November 18 memorandum during Secretary Hull’s absence. He expresses appreciation for the Association’s interest and emphasizes the Department’s continuing concern with narcotics control.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 4313: Japanese Narcotics Traffic Report, 1938
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Grew transmits two copies of the Japanese Government’s official narcotics report for 1938.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy reports that it recently received the official Japanese report from the Foreign Office. Grew encloses two English-language copies of the Annual Report on the Traffic in Opium and Other Dangerous Drugs for 1938.

subfiles.title: Annual Report on the Traffic in Opium and Other Dangerous Drugs for 1938—Japan Proper section
subfiles.about: This portion of Japan’s 1938 annual report details narcotics regulation, addiction, enforcement, cultivation, seizures, and manufacture in Japan Proper.
subfiles.summary: The report states that narcotics administration passed to the Ministry of Welfare in January 1938 and records 3,600 addicts, including patients treated at Musashino Hospital. It describes international certificate controls, information exchange with the United States and Great Britain, 49 offense cases involving 112 offenders, and confiscation of more than 80 kilograms of opium and dangerous drugs. Further sections give statistics on licensed opium-poppy and coca cultivation and list authorized manufacturers in Tokyo, Osaka, and Shizuoka. The report attributes increased legitimate narcotics manufacture partly to medical demand in Japanese-occupied China.
